::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, November 2026.** A short, philosophical essay on what AI means for discovery. It starts from Poincaré's view that scientists pursue the harmony they sense in nature [@poincare1914], and from Iain McGilchrist's claim that great discoveries are not made by following the scientific method [@mcgilchrist2026]. The one figure is a schematic of my own, drawn with the code in [figs.py](figs.py).
:::

**In short.** Ask an AI what to try next in research, and it will give a sensible answer, close to what the field already believes. It does exactly what the scientific method asks: rank ideas by how plausible they look, and test the best first. AI is that method, perfected. But the discoveries that change a field are often the ones that looked least plausible, and their evidence arrives only after years of work that seems to lead nowhere. Reaching them takes something the method does not hold: a sense that an unlikely idea is beautiful enough to be true, and the faith to stay with it in the dark. AI does not remove that need. It makes it plainer. Machines can tell us what is likely. Deciding what is worth believing long enough to prove it is still up to us.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Key takeaways

- AI trained on what science has written ranks ideas the way the field already does, faster and more evenly than any of us. That is the method, perfected.
- Great discoveries tend to rank last: implausible to the experts, and silent for years before the evidence comes.
- What carries them through is taste, a sense of harmony the literature does not contain, and faith, belief held long enough to reach the test.
- Faith without taste is only stubbornness. Most believers are wrong; without them, the right few are never tested.
- If testing became cheap enough to try every idea, faith would matter less. That may happen in games, code and proofs. In open science, the world sets the pace of tests.
:::

## 1. The best rule-follower ever made

Ask a capable model what to try next in a research programme, and the answer will be good. It will be well argued, well referenced, and close to what the field already believes. This is not a flaw. The model learned from what the field has written, and it was rewarded for answers that experts rate as good. It does exactly what we asked.

This is also what we were taught the scientific method is: careful rules, reduction to parts, plausible hypotheses tested in order. If that were the whole of science, AI would soon be its best practitioner, and some systems already try to run the whole loop, from idea to paper [@lu2024].

I think AI is something more precise than a new scientist. It is the method, perfected. It ranks the world by what we already find plausible, and it will make us much faster at that. Which raises the question I want to ask in this essay: what about the discoveries that were never plausible?

## 2. The ideas the method ranks last

In the early 1980s, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed that a bacterium causes stomach ulcers. Most experts believed that bacteria could not live in the acid of the stomach, and that ulcers came from stress and acid. Their paper met disbelief [@marshall1984]. Marshall ended up drinking a culture of the bacterium to show that it made him ill. The two received the Nobel Prize in 2005.

In the same years, Dan Shechtman saw a crystal pattern that the textbooks said could not exist [@shechtman1984]. For years he was told he was wrong, and he was asked to leave his research group. He received the Nobel Prize in 2011.

The pattern is common enough to have names. Thomas Kuhn called it the difference between puzzle-solving inside a shared frame and the revolutions that change the frame [@kuhn1962]. A saying attributed to Max Planck holds that science advances one funeral at a time, and economists have found that, when a star scientist dies, outsiders do enter the field and publish work that is cited more [@azoulay2019]. Highly novel papers are more likely to end up among the most cited, but they are recognised late [@wang2017].

What these stories share is a stretch of time I think of as the dark period. The idea is on the table, but the decisive evidence is years away. In between, the signals are weak, noisy and often discouraging. Any careful person, following the rules, would move on. Figure 1 is how I picture it.

![**Figure 1.** An idea the field expects gathers evidence quickly. An idea it does not expect goes through a dark period, where the evidence wanders and often falls below the point where a careful method would move on. Only someone who keeps going reaches the test. Schematic, my own.](figures/fig01.svg){fig-alt="A chart of evidence for an idea against time spent on it. A blue curve, an idea the consensus expects, rises quickly and levels off. A purple curve, an idea the consensus does not expect, wanders near zero through a shaded dark period labelled no decisive evidence yet. It dips below a red dashed line labelled below this line, the method moves on. Then it rises steeply above the blue curve after the dark period ends. A label says conviction carries it to the decisive test."}

Now give that careful person an AI. It is cheaper and faster, so it can work further down the list of ideas. But it works down the same list, in the same order, because the list is the field's own sense of what is plausible. AI moves the method along the consensus. It does not move it across.

## 3. Beauty as a sieve

So what makes someone stay with an idea through the dark? Poincaré gave an answer more than a century ago. The scientist, he wrote, "does not study nature because it is useful to do so. He studies it because he takes pleasure in it, and he takes pleasure in it because it is beautiful" [@poincare1914, Book I, ch. 1]. He did not mean the beauty of appearances. He meant the harmony among the parts, which the mind grasps.

In his chapter on mathematical discovery he went further. Among the countless combinations an inventor could try, he argued, a sense of elegance acts as a sieve. It lets through to awareness the few combinations worth checking [@poincare1914, Book I, ch. 3]. On this view, taste is not decoration on top of discovery. It is how discovery chooses where to look.

Michael Polanyi made a similar point in another language. All knowing, he argued, involves personal commitment, and "intellectual passions" decide which problems are worth a life [@polanyi1958]. More recently, Iain McGilchrist has argued that the great advances came from breaking the rules rather than following them, and from seeing the world whole rather than only in parts [@mcgilchrist2026]. I share his conclusion, without needing his account of the brain's two hemispheres, which is debated.

Taste, in this sense, is a signal the literature does not contain. If it were written down, it would already be part of the consensus, and the method would use it.

## 4. Faith, narrowly

The word faith makes scientists uneasy, so let me say exactly what I mean. Faith here is belief in an idea beyond what the evidence yet supports, together with the will to act on it for a long time. It is closer to Polanyi's commitment than to religion.

The strongest objection is obvious. For every Marshall, many people believed against the evidence and were simply wrong. Survivors tell the story; the others are forgotten. I accept this completely. Most faith in science is misplaced, and faith without taste is only stubbornness.

But the argument does not need believers to be right most of the time. It needs only this: without them, the right few are never tested. A field where nobody is willing to spend years on an idea the field doubts will never find out which of those ideas were true. The method cannot do it, because its whole virtue is to follow what looks likely.

Here is my real claim, and it is a belief rather than a result. I suspect that, at the edges of every field, the consensus is wrong in a systematic way. Some kinds of far-fetched ideas turn out true more often than experts expect, and nothing written beforehand tells which ones. If that is so, then no amount of better ranking reaches them. Only someone who believes first does.

## 5. Could cheap testing make faith unnecessary?

There is a serious way this argument could fail, and it comes from AI itself. Faith matters because testing is expensive. If testing an idea became nearly free, nobody would need to believe in anything first. We would test everything, and the unlikely ideas would be checked along with the rest. Call it a singularity of discovery: the point where search is so cheap that ranking, and therefore faith, stops mattering.

In some places this may already be happening. In games, in code, in mathematics with proof checkers, in protein structure, the goal is fixed and an answer can be checked in seconds. There machines search enormous spaces, and they have already gone beyond the consensus: AlphaGo's successors played moves no strong human would have played [@silver2017], and AlphaTensor found ways to multiply matrices that people had missed [@fawzi2022]. In those domains, I expect faith to matter less and less.

Open science is different, for three reasons. The space of ideas grows with knowledge: every answer opens new questions, so there is always more to test than any budget can cover. Many tests have a physical pace that computation cannot shorten, such as a ten-year trial, a new instrument, or the slow change of a field's mind. And only ideas that someone proposes ever get tested. If models propose ideas close to what is already believed, the far ones never enter the queue, however cheap testing becomes. There is already a hint of this: experts rated research ideas written by a language model as more novel than their own, but the model's ideas varied little from one to the next [@si2025].

So I do not expect one singularity for all of science. I expect it domain by domain, where checking is fast. Everywhere else, the dark period stays dark.

## 6. What AI represents

If this is right, AI stands for three things at once.

**A mirror.** Much of what we used to call doing science is search, recombination and checking inside a frame. Machines now do that well. Seeing it done well shows how much of our work was this part, and what is left.

**A risk of convergence.** When everyone consults the same models, trained on the same literature, everyone ranks ideas in the same order. Each researcher gets better while the field as a whole narrows. A study of millions of papers found exactly this pattern: scientists who use AI publish more and are cited more, while AI-heavy research covers a narrower range of topics [@hao2024]. Writers who use AI write better stories that resemble each other more [@doshi2024]. Planck's saying needed funerals for science to move on. A consensus held by a model has no one to bury.

**An opportunity.** If machines carry the method, ordinary work gets cheaper, and the savings could pay for long, unlikely bets. That will happen only if someone chooses it. The default is more of the same, because the same is what the method ranks first.

## 7. How I could be wrong

Two things would prove this essay wrong. If the consensus is right even at its edges, so that far-fetched ideas turn out true no more often than experts expect, then the method is all discovery needs, and faith is only a story we tell afterwards. And if the signal that separates the right far ideas from the wrong ones is already in the literature, a good enough model will find it, and taste adds nothing.

Both can be checked, at least in principle. One could give a model only the literature written before a past breakthrough and see whether it would have dismissed the idea, and whether it could tell it apart from the far ideas that failed. I would like to see that experiment run. Until then, this is a conviction, which seems fitting.

## 8. In the dark

What I take from all this is practical. Use the machine for what it does best: the search, the checking, the long list of plausible next steps. Then keep some time, and some budget, for one idea you find beautiful and that nobody else believes yet. Expect to be wrong most of the time. Stay with it long enough to find out.

Machines can tell us what is likely. Deciding what is worth believing long enough to prove it is still up to us.
